h1: Your Team Saved 20 Minutes. The Customer Waited Another Day.
seo_title: How to Measure a Workflow Improvement | NATA
meta_description: Compare handling time, elapsed time, accuracy, and downstream work with a practical before-and-after example for a service business.
section_questions: Which numbers show what really improved?
How do you measure whether work moved to another team?
How do you decide whether the time saved is worth anything?
answer_capsule: To measure a workflow improvement, define a comparable case and record elapsed time, employee effort, quality, and what happens next. Include the people who absorb extra work. Compare the same kinds of cases before and after, and decide upfront which result would make the company keep, change, or stop the intervention.
takeaways: The point where the buyer or next team can actually use the output.
Time and corrections across the people doing the work.
The condition that would make you expand, change, or stop the pilot.

faqs.question: How many cases are enough to assess a change?
faqs.answer: Use enough cases to see common variations and important exceptions. A small sample can reveal a failure and help choose a next test. A larger or longer comparison is useful when volume, seasonality, or job mix makes the effect hard to distinguish.

faqs.question: Is average completion time enough?
faqs.answer: Look at the distribution, missed deadlines, and quality as well. Check whether the same types of cases went into each group.

faqs.question: How do you attribute the change to one tool?
faqs.answer: Keep other conditions as stable as practical and document what else changed. A comparison against a similar group or a staggered trial can help. Treat observational results with the limits their setup warrants.
